source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter I, §4 Some Winning Positions in the Middle-game, Example 11

steps.title: Now with all the pieces
steps.source: Before considering the openings, we shall devote a little time to some combinations that often arise during the game, and which will give the reader some idea of the beauty of the game.

narration.say: Now a real middle-game position. It is Black's move.
White seems to threaten queen to h6, and mate on g7 with the help of the bishop.
Black thinks that is the only threat, and plays rook to e8, threatening mate on e1.
But White has a much stronger threat. Can you find it?

exercise.prompt: White to move. Find the hidden threat.

feedback.Qh6: Too slow: Black mates first with Re1 check.
feedback.*: Look for a sacrifice that opens the h-file for the rook.

exercise.hint: The queen takes a pawn, with check.
exercise.success: 2. Qxh7, check! The black king must take.

narration.say: The h-file is open. Bring the rook.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Check with the rook.

feedback.*: The rook swings to the h-file with check.

exercise.hint: The rook moves along the third rank.
exercise.success: 3. Rh3, check. Black goes back to g8.

exercise.prompt: White to move and give checkmate in one.

feedback.*: The rook goes all the way up the h-file.

exercise.hint: The rook reaches the eighth rank.
exercise.success: Checkmate. The bishop on b2 controls g7, so the king has no escape.

narration.say: Before answering a threat, look for the opponent's real, most effective threat.
Here the bishop on the long diagonal and the rook on the h-file worked together against the king.
